MorphSkein: A Shape-Changing Afterimage Display Preserving Pixel Density During Surface-Area Changes Across Troposkein-Based Shapes
problem Spinning displays can show pictures in 360 degrees, but expanding their size stretches pixels and makes them look bad.
approach Spin cables on a pole using careful physics and timing to create expanding shapes while releasing new pixel rows to keep density steady.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

A shape-changing display tries to make pixels occupy a physical surface that can change form. The ordinary problem is that when the surface gets larger, the same number of lights must cover more area, so the image becomes sparse. MorphSkein tackles that problem for a display made from spinning LED strips. As the strips rotate, persistence of vision makes the viewer see a continuous 360-degree display, and centrifugal force bends the strips into troposkein shapes. A troposkein is the natural curve made by a spinning cable under its own motion. The system can change shape by adjusting a telescopic pole and the strip lengths. The paper's key purpose is to preserve the initial pixel density, stated as 1.44 pixels per square centimeter, as surface area changes. The visual goal is not only to make a moving sculpture, but to keep displayed imagery from thinning out as the physical display expands.

why it's hard

The hard part is that surface area and pixel count are tied together. If a display stretches while using the same exposed LEDs and the same columns per spin, each pixel covers more physical space. The image loses density, especially around the expanded middle of the shape. MorphSkein also cannot freely place pixels anywhere; it uses four LED strips on rewinders, a rotating base, a pole, motor speed, microcontroller speed, and LED refresh rate. The physical shape depends on angular velocity, because the spinning speed affects the cable curve. The image density depends on how many rows are released and how many columns can be drawn per revolution. Those needs can conflict. An incorrect speed can damage density accuracy, shape fidelity, or both. The paper therefore has to coordinate mechanics, timing, and a mathematical shape model rather than simply scaling an image.

the naive solution

A beginner might build the spinning strip display, change its shape by letting out more cable, and render the same image samples as before. That fails because the expanded surface spreads the same pixels over a larger area. Another attempt would be to add more LEDs everywhere, but the system is constrained by strips, rewinders, motor limits, controller speed, and refresh rate. A third attempt is to adjust only the image horizontally by drawing more columns each revolution. That helps around the spin direction but does not add vertical rows along the strips. MorphSkein needs both vertical and horizontal density control, and those controls must respect the physical curve.

the core idea

MorphSkein preserves density by adding display samples in the two directions where expansion would otherwise thin them out. Vertically, as the surface area grows, the rewinders release new rows of LEDs from the strips. Horizontally, the renderer draws extra columns during each revolution. The physical system uses a telescopic pole and four LED-strip rewinders on a rotating base. Changing pole height and strip length changes the troposkein shape. The display is visible around 360 degrees because persistence of vision blends fast LED flashes into a continuous surface in the viewer's eye. The method relies on a mathematical model of ideal troposkein geometry to decide which operating speeds and lengths can preserve both shape and density. Experimental interpolation then identifies which reachable configurations achieve at least 90 percent density accuracy and shape fidelity for at least one operating speed.

how the mechanism runs

The input is a desired axisymmetric display shape within the family of troposkein-based forms, along with the image content to show and the initial density target of 1.44 pixels per square centimeter. The mechanism starts by setting the telescopic pole height and the lengths of the four LED strips using rewinders. When the base spins, centrifugal force pulls the strips outward into curved troposkein shapes. The LEDs flash as they rotate, and persistence of vision makes separate flashes appear as a continuous 360-degree display. As the surface area grows, the system releases additional LED rows from the rewinders so the vertical spacing of samples does not stretch too far. It also renders extra columns per revolution, increasing the number of angular samples around the display. The density is described as comparable along the central horizontal line, while the top and bottom naturally receive higher density because the troposkein curves inward there. The method uses an ideal troposkein model to predict the relation among pole height, strip length, angular velocity, shape, and density. Because real hardware has limits, the paper interpolates experimental data to find reachable configurations and operating speeds. The output is a shape-changing afterimage display whose density and shape fidelity are measured across those configurations.

mathematical concepts

The mathematical object is a rotating curve. A cable spinning around an axis settles into a troposkein shape because tension and centrifugal force must balance along its length. Axisymmetry means the shape is the same around the central axis, so a curve swept through rotation becomes a surface. Pixel density is a counting-per-area idea: how many visible samples occupy each square centimeter of that surface. When surface area increases, density falls unless the number of samples increases too. MorphSkein controls samples in two directions. Along the strip, it releases more LED rows. Around the axis, it draws more columns per revolution. Angular velocity, the spin speed, is a key variable because it affects both the physical curve and the time available for drawing columns in each cycle. Interpolation appears as a practical mathematical tool: measured data at some configurations is used to estimate behavior between them. The tradeoff is shape fidelity versus density accuracy versus hardware speed and timing. A configuration is useful only if the mechanics form the desired curve and the electronics can refresh enough pixels at that speed.

connecting the dots

This paper connects to display research because it works around the eye: persistence of vision turns a moving line of LEDs into a surface. It connects to physical simulation and geometry because the display shape is not arbitrary; it comes from the mechanics of a spinning cable and an axisymmetric surface. It also connects to fabrication and hardware-aware graphics, where the image cannot be separated from motor speed, controller limits, and material motion. Neighboring SIGGRAPH work on rendering asks how to place light samples in an image; this paper asks how to place visible samples on a changing physical surface. The shared idea is sampling under constraints. The system must decide where and when samples appear so the viewer perceives a stable image while the physical display changes area.

why it works

MorphSkein should preserve density better than simply stretching the same display because it attacks the two sources of thinning separately. When the surface grows vertically, more LED rows are physically released, so the strip direction gains more samples. When the circumference-like direction needs more detail, the renderer adds columns during each revolution, so the sweep direction gains more samples. The ideal troposkein model matters because the surface area and curvature are not arbitrary; they depend on the spinning cable shape. Using that model lets the system choose operating conditions rather than guessing. The experimental interpolation matters because real motors, controllers, and LED strips do not behave like perfect equations. The method works when there is at least one angular velocity at which the desired shape and the needed refresh pattern are both feasible. That explains why some configurations succeed and others degrade because motor speed, microcontroller speed, or LED refresh rate is insufficient.

the payoff

The payoff is a shape-changing afterimage display that can preserve its initial density across many troposkein-based shapes instead of visibly thinning as area expands. The abstract reports 1.44 pixels per square centimeter as the preserved initial density target. It also says 69.44 percent of reachable troposkein configurations achieve at least 90 percent density accuracy and shape fidelity for at least one operating speed. The result is a concrete hardware method for changing display shape while keeping image sampling comparable along the central horizontal line.

limits and assumptions

The method is limited by its physical and timing assumptions. It relies on an ideal troposkein geometry model, so real cable behavior must be close enough for the predictions to hold. Angular velocity is critical: wrong speeds can reduce density accuracy, shape fidelity, or both. The density is comparable along the central horizontal line, while the top and bottom have naturally higher density because the curve narrows there, so uniformity is not identical everywhere. The abstract states remaining failures come from insufficient motor speed or limited microcontroller speed and LED refresh rate.

StyleID: A Perception-Aware Dataset and Metric for Stylization-Agnostic Facial Identity Recognition
problem Face-recognition systems fail when a photo is drawn as a cartoon or painting because they learned on real photos and can't adapt to style changes.
approach New test-and-tune sets measure human judgment of faces across styles, then train systems to match how people actually recognize identity through artistic distortion.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

Face stylization changes a portrait into a cartoon, sketch, painting, or other visual idiom while trying to keep the person recognizable. That is harder than it sounds because identity is not stored in one obvious place. People use facial geometry, relative feature placement, characteristic shapes, and sometimes texture cues, but a style can deliberately alter colors, lines, proportions, and surface detail. Existing machine identity encoders are usually trained on natural photographs, so they can confuse style changes with identity changes. The paper introduces StyleID to measure and supervise identity consistency across styles in a way that follows human perception. It builds one dataset from human same-different judgments under multiple style strengths and another from controlled two-choice experiments that measure recognition strength. Those data are then used to tune existing encoders so their similarity ordering better matches how people judge identity across stylized portraits.

why it's hard

The central tension is that stylization is supposed to change appearance while identity is supposed to remain stable. A photo-trained identity model often learns shortcuts that work in ordinary photos: skin texture, color distribution, photographic shading, and natural feature proportions. Stylization breaks those shortcuts on purpose. The abstract says current encoders can be brittle in two opposite ways. They may treat a new texture or color palette as identity drift even when a human still sees the same person. Or they may fail to notice geometric exaggerations, where the style changes the shapes and spacing that humans rely on for recognition. A useful measure must separate style strength from identity loss, but those effects are tangled. As styles become stronger, human certainty may gradually fall rather than flip at one clean boundary. That is why the paper uses human judgments and recognition-strength curves instead of assuming photo similarity is enough.

the naive solution

A simple solution is to run a normal face-recognition encoder on the original portrait and the stylized result, then compare the two feature vectors. If the numbers are close, call the identity preserved; if not, call it changed. That is tempting because such encoders already exist and work well on photographs. The failure is that their notion of closeness may not match human recognition outside photos. They can punish harmless changes in paint texture, line style, or color, and they can overlook shape exaggerations that make a face feel like someone else. Another naive option is to ask humans every time, but that is too slow to supervise many stylization systems.

the core idea

The paper's central move is to make human perception the reference point for identity under style. StyleBench-H records same-different verification judgments from people across stylized faces made at multiple style strengths. StyleBench-S is a supervision set derived from psychometric recognition-strength curves, which means the data track how recognition changes gradually as the visual evidence becomes easier or harder, using controlled two-alternative forced-choice experiments. With that supervision, the authors fine-tune existing semantic encoders so that their similarity rankings agree better with human orderings across styles and strengths. In plain terms, the model is taught that two portraits can look very different in texture while still being the same person, and that some shape changes are more identity-damaging than their surface style might suggest.

how the mechanism runs

The input is a collection of portraits stylized in different visual idioms and at different strengths, along with human judgments about whether pairs show the same person. For StyleBench-H, people provide same-different decisions, giving a direct record of human verification under style changes. For StyleBench-S, controlled two-choice experiments produce recognition-strength curves, which describe not only a yes-or-no answer but how recognition changes as the stylization varies. The method then takes existing semantic encoders, meaning models that turn an image into a compact description intended to capture meaningful face information, and adjusts them using StyleBench-S. The comparison target is the human ordering: if people find one stylized portrait closer in identity than another, the encoder should rank those similarities the same way. After training, the encoder can score new stylized portraits by comparing their internal descriptions. The output is an evaluation and supervision tool for identity consistency under stylization. The abstract says experiments show higher correlation with human judgments and better behavior on artist-drawn portraits outside the original domain, but the provided text cuts off before the full final phrase. The useful internal check is ranking, not just classification: the model must put examples in the same near-to-far order that people do, which is a stricter demand than merely naming a pair same or different.

mathematical concepts

The main mathematical idea is similarity ordering. Instead of asking whether two images have identical pixels, the method asks whether their learned descriptions lie close in a space where distance is meant to reflect perceived identity. A feature space is simply a coordinate system built by a model: each image becomes a list of numbers, and nearby lists are supposed to mean similar content. The problem is that a photo-trained coordinate system may put style changes in the same directions as identity changes. StyleID uses human judgments to reshape that space. Psychometric curves add another idea: perception can be measured as a gradual response, not only as correct or incorrect. A recognition-strength curve records how likely people are to identify a face as style strength changes. Fine-tuning is adjustment by error: the encoder's ordering is compared with human ordering, and its settings are changed so future distances better match those judgments. The tradeoff is style freedom versus identity trust, with human perception defining the balance. The important principle is calibration: a distance only becomes meaningful when its units match the judgment people care about. Here the paper changes the measuring stick so one step in feature space means closer to one step in perceived identity, even when style changes the pixels.

connecting the dots

This paper connects to image generation, face editing, and evaluation. Many stylization papers can create striking portraits, but they need a way to tell whether the person survived the style change. It also sits near reconstruction and recognition work, where a machine must decide which visual evidence is essential and which is accidental. The broader SIGGRAPH idea is that appearance is layered: color, texture, drawing style, shape, and identity can move together or apart. Neighboring generation methods based on learned image models can vary style strength smoothly, which makes a gradual human-aligned metric important. The paper is less about inventing a new stylizer than about building the measuring stick that lets stylization systems be compared, supervised, and trusted when ordinary photo-based identity scores fail.

why it works

The method should work better because it trains the measure on the exact confusion the task creates. A normal identity encoder has learned from natural photographs, where texture, color, and geometry usually follow familiar patterns. Stylized portraits deliberately violate those patterns. By collecting human judgments across style types and strengths, StyleID observes which changes people tolerate and which changes make identity fade. The two-choice recognition curves are especially useful because they describe degrees of recognition, so the model is not forced into a brittle all-or-nothing target. Fine-tuning the encoder to match human similarity orderings then changes what its distances mean: style differences that people ignore should count less, and geometry changes that people notice should count more. The improvement is causal only to the extent that the collected judgments cover the kinds of stylization the calibrated model later sees. That makes the learned distance less like a photo detector and more like a ruler for the particular human question: would this still be recognized as the same face?

the payoff

The payoff is a more human-aligned way to evaluate and supervise face stylization. The paper provides StyleBench-H for human same-different judgments and StyleBench-S for supervision from recognition-strength curves. It reports that calibrated models correlate better with human judgments and are more reliable for portraits outside the ordinary photo domain, including artist-drawn cases named in the abstract. That gives stylization systems a clearer target than photo-trained identity similarity alone. This matters because identity preservation is often the hidden constraint behind creative portrait tools, yet ordinary photo similarity can punish exactly the style changes the user wanted.

limits and assumptions

The method assumes the collected human judgments represent the intended viewers and style range. If a future style changes identity cues in a way not covered by the data, the tuned encoder may still fail. The abstract names diffusion- and flow-matching-based stylization, meaning learned image generators that transform pictures through gradual model steps, but it does not prove coverage of all artistic media. It also reports improved correlation, not perfect agreement, and the provided batch text is truncated before the full out-of-domain result description.

Fabrication & 3D Printing 6

Problem. Turning a virtual design into a real physical object runs headlong into what machines can actually make — a printer or knitting machine can only produce certain shapes. Approach. Plan the design backward from the machine's real limits, so what you model on screen can actually be built faithfully.

read this paper family from first principles
problem shape

This family is about the moment when a computer design has to become a physical thing. On screen, a surface can bend freely, pass through itself by accident, use impossible layers, or ignore how stress travels. In the world, a printer nozzle has a size, a resin blurs as light and chemistry spread, fabric plies need manufacturable thickness, architectural panels must carry load, and a virtual object can feel real only if some nearby physical object can stand in for it. The shared problem is not just making a shape. It is converting intent into a build plan that respects matter. Each paper asks what must stay true during that conversion: a composite should become stiffer, a freeform surface should keep its look while lowering stress, a triangle surface should stop crossing through itself, a filament printer should follow continuous bead paths, a VR touch target should match a real object, and a holographic printer should deposit enough curing dose in the right tiny places. The family exists because fabrication exposes every hidden lie in a digital model.

why the naive attempt fails

A smart beginner would first separate design from making. Draw the best-looking surface, then panelize it. Pick a strong composite layout, then cut fabric layers afterward. Slice a print into ordinary flat layers, then ask the nozzle to follow them. Remove surface crossings by pushing apart only the visibly colliding triangles. For touch in VR, print a matching prop or use visual feedback alone. For holographic printing, compute the light pattern and ignore how the resin keeps reacting after light arrives. These ideas fail because physical constraints are coupled. Changing a panel changes stress elsewhere. A fabric boundary changes stiffness across neighboring layers. A local untangle can create a larger knot. A nozzle path must preserve bead thickness, avoid collisions, and keep moving. A room object must match shape, position, and touch qualities. In resin, optics and chemistry blur together.

mathematical principle

The recurring mathematical principle is to turn fabrication into a scored agreement among many promises. A promise can be geometric: the surface should stay close to the intended form, should not pass through itself, and should be split into usable panels or layers. A promise can be mechanical: stress should be lowered, stiffness should rise, and material directions should carry force well. A promise can be machine-related: the filament bead should keep nearly constant thickness, the tool should not collide, and non-printing travel should be small. A promise can be sensory or chemical: a real object should match a virtual touch target, or a hologram should create a dose pattern that survives light bending and inhibitor diffusion. The method then adjusts the design, layer fields, paths, surface positions, hologram sequence, or object match to reduce the measured violations. This is optimization, meaning repeated score-and-adjust search, but the score is not abstract. It is a checklist of what would break in fabrication. The key tradeoff is design freedom versus physical obedience: enough freedom to improve shape, touch, stiffness, or resolution, but enough obedience that the result can actually be made or used.

why the math matters

The math matters because fabrication constraints are spread out, not isolated. Stress is global: a weak region may be caused by panel choices far away because load travels through the whole shell. Composite layers are directional: a fabric ply can be strong along one direction and weaker across another, so partial layer boundaries change how force moves between layers. Self-intersection is also global. A triangle surface, meaning a skin made of many flat patches, can be locally separated in one place yet still folded through itself as a whole. Filament printing is path-based: every point on a layer affects the next point because the nozzle must move continuously with a fixed bead profile. Holographic resin printing is coupled through light waves and chemistry: the projected phase pattern bends light, while curing and inhibitor diffusion smear the final solid. ProXeek uses the same logic in a different material setting: the physical room already contains objects, but a match is useful only when several constraints agree at once. Mathematics gives these papers a way to see long-range consequences before a machine or user exposes the mistake.

the paper family

The papers are siblings because each replaces an after-the-fact repair step with a coupled making plan. Co-Optimization of Structure and Manufacturable Semi-Continuous Layers for Laminated Composites does not first choose a shape and later decide fabric plies. It adjusts structure and manufacturable partial layers together, modeling how layer boundaries change directional mechanical behavior, and reports higher stiffness than planar ply counterparts. Stress-Aware Panelization makes a similar move for architecture: instead of panelizing a freeform surface and only then checking strength, it lets stress analysis influence the surface flow while preserving design intent. Untangling Surfaces handles the prerequisite for many fabrication pipelines: the digital skin must be embedded, meaning it occupies space without crossing through itself, so the method uses both broad shape repulsion and local triangle-level penalties. AtomSlicer turns multi-axis filament printing into a path agreement problem, preserving orientation fields, near-constant layer thickness, continuous toolpaths, and collision avoidance, or reporting that the request cannot be fabricated. Single-View Holographic Volumetric 3D Printing couples wave optics with resin chemistry so the light plan pre-compensates for chemical blur. ProXeek broadens fabrication into opportunistic touch: rather than making a prop, it matches virtual interactables to real objects already in the room.

what changed in 2026

The 2026 pattern is that fabrication papers are moving from shape-first pipelines toward constraint-first pipelines. The evidence emphasizes joint design and manufacturing instead of cleanup after design is frozen. Composite layout, panel stress, surface untangling, multi-axis slicing, holographic curing, and VR haptic proxy selection all treat fabrication limits as part of the main computation. Another change is stronger honesty about feasibility. AtomSlicer preserves user or solver-defined fields and reports non-fabricability rather than quietly changing the request. The holographic printer models both optics and chemistry rather than only the projected light. ProXeek compares real room objects against touch constraints instead of assuming a custom printed replica is the best physical answer.

limits and assumptions

These results depend on the chosen physical models and inputs. Composite design assumes the layer field, stiffness model, and manufacturing objectives describe the real fabric plies well enough. Stress-aware panelization depends on the shell model, stress objective, and architectural shapes tested. Untangling assumes the surface representation can be moved without changing connectivity and that repulsion energies capture the relevant crossings. AtomSlicer assumes supplied orientation fields, bead profile, and machine collision checks match the printer. Holographic volumetric printing is shown on small volumes and simple structures, with simplified photochemistry. ProXeek depends on headset snapshots, annotations, language-model reasoning, and available room objects. The evidence reports selected validations, not universal guarantees across all materials, printers, rooms, scales, noise levels, or manufacturing tolerances.

Single-View Holographic Volumetric 3D Printing with Coupled Differentiable Wave-Optical and Photochemical Optimization
problem 3D printing with light needs to create tiny details, but light bends and spreads, and chemicals diffuse, both blurring the result.
approach They designed light patterns from a single direction that pre-correct for how light will bend and chemicals will blur during printing.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

3D printing usually builds objects layer by layer, which is slow. Volumetric additive manufacturing aims to harden an entire 3D volume at once using light and chemistry, potentially printing complex shapes in seconds. Achieving fine detail (10 micrometers or finer) requires precise control of where light hits and how the chemistry responds, and that requires solving an inverse problem: given a desired shape, what hologram (light pattern) do you project?

why it's hard

Light diffracts—it bends around edges—making the projected pattern not match the desired shape exactly. Additionally, the liquid resin does not harden instantly; inhibitor chemicals diffuse, blur the boundary, and further obscure the pattern. Optimizing the hologram naively only accounts for light optics and ignores the chemistry, leading to blurry prints.

the core idea

The team formulates hologram synthesis as coupled inverse problem: they build a differentiable model of wave-optical diffraction and a simplified photochemical model capturing inhibitor diffusion and nonlinear dose response. They then optimize the hologram sequence to minimize the discrepancy between the predicted hardened shape and the desired shape.

why it works

By modeling both the wave optics (how light diffracts) and the photochemistry (how inhibitor spreads and how resin hardens nonlinearly), you can predict the final hardened shape more accurately. This allows you to pre-compensate in the hologram—designing the light pattern to overshoot in places where chemistry will blur it, so the final result matches the target shape.

the payoff

Single-view holographic 3D printing can now achieve finer detail (10 micrometers) in seconds by compensating for both optical and chemical blur, enabling volumetric manufacturing of small, high-fidelity parts.

Sketching & Vector / 2D 6

Problem. A great deal of art is still made by drawing, and digital tools that ignore how an artist actually works — in strokes, lines, and shapes — get in the way. Approach. Build drawing and flat-graphics tools that meet artists in their own idiom, turning sketches and strokes into clean, editable, expressive results.

read this paper family from first principles
problem shape

This family is about drawings that must behave like structured objects, not just colored marks on a page. A stroke in an animation may pass behind another stroke and reappear later. A curve cut out of a three-dimensional scene may need to say clearly which line is in front. A smooth color boundary in vector art may need to spread tone across a region without breaking at the edge. A texture pasted on a shape may need to survive later edits to that shape. The shared pressure is that two-dimensional visual work often has hidden order underneath it: layers, crossings, surfaces, color boundaries, and time. A flat picture can look simple to the viewer while being hard for a computer because the drawing has to remember which parts connect, which parts block others, and which changes preserve the intended appearance. These papers belong together because they try to turn hand-drawn or vector-like marks into reliable structures that can be animated, intersected, rendered, edited, or connected back to three-dimensional form.

why the naive attempt fails

A smart first attempt would treat every visible line or color patch as independent. For animation, match each stroke in one drawing to the nearest stroke in the next drawing and blend their positions. For 3D vectorization, project curves onto the image and sort them afterward. For surface intersections, sample many points and connect the ones that seem close. For textured shapes, edit the shape and hope the texture follows. These shortcuts fail when important information is hidden at the exact places where drawings are most useful: crossings, tangencies, occlusions, small loops, and boundaries. Nearby strokes may not be the same object. A line can disappear because it is behind another line, not because it ends. Tiny intersection loops can be missed by sparse sampling. Texture coordinates can preserve a picture poorly after the shape is changed. The failure is not just visual mess; it is loss of the relationships that make the drawing editable.

mathematical principle

The repeated mathematical idea is to replace loose pixels or loose strokes with relationships that can be checked. Some papers ask what should stay connected as a line moves through time. Some ask how a flat plane is divided when many projected curves cross. Some ask whether a tiny closed intersection loop exists even when ordinary point sampling misses it. Some ask how color should spread from boundary curves into the empty space between them. In everyday terms, the math acts like bookkeeping for promises: this stroke continues here, this region lies in front of that one, this curve enters and leaves a patch, this surface color should remain attached to the visible shape, and this color field should satisfy the boundary conditions set by the drawn curves. The tools differ. Winding numbers count how a path wraps around a point so hidden loops can be detected. Subdivision repeatedly cuts a hard region into smaller regions until its structure is easier to decide. Monte Carlo sampling spends random trials on estimating many small contributions instead of tracing every possible influence. The common tradeoff is freedom versus consistency: artists want flexible marks, but the computer needs enough structure to avoid broken crossings, wrong layers, and unstable edits.

why the math matters

The math matters because vector and sketch-like graphics are full of exact-looking events that are easy to damage. A crossing is not just two dark marks touching; it decides which curve continues, which region is separated, and which part may be hidden. A tangent contact, where two surfaces just brush, can be more fragile than a clean crossing because a tiny numerical error can turn contact into a miss or a false overlap. A diffusion curve is not only a line with colors on its sides; it asks the surrounding area to fill itself smoothly from those boundary instructions. A texture on a shape is not merely an image pasted on top; later tools must know how the appearance travels with the shape. These papers need counting, partitioning, repeated refinement, and solving because the important facts are relational. They live between marks: inside or outside, before or behind, connected or separated, preserved or changed. Hand-written rules tend to fail at special cases, while mathematical checks give the system a way to notice when several visual promises must all be true at once.

the paper family

LayerInbetween represents the time side of the family: it treats inbetweening as more than sliding strokes between drawings, because occluded strokes require a predicted layer order and a correspondence between marks that may not always be visible. Robust Planar Maps for 3D Vectorization represents the projection side: it turns curve soup from a three-dimensional scene into a valid flat division, so lines, intersections, and occlusions can be handled as an organized map rather than as independent curves. The NURBS surface intersection paper handles a related crossing problem on smooth designed surfaces, where small loops and tangent intersections can vanish unless the method reasons about wrapping and subdivides the search carefully. Texture-Aware Remeshing moves the same concern into surface editing: it tries to keep appearance attached to geometry by carrying texture information onto vertices before later processing. Monte Carlo Rendering of Biharmonic Diffusion Curves handles the color-spreading side of vector graphics, using random estimates and a solved boundary problem to render smooth fields from curve instructions. Across these examples, the deeper move is the same: turn a drawing-like object into a structure whose hidden connections, regions, and boundary promises can survive computation.

what changed in 2026

The 2026 version of this family seems less focused on making vector graphics merely cleaner and more focused on making them dependable under hard operations. The evidence points to occlusion-aware animation, valid planar maps for projected 3D curves, intersection handling for tiny loops and tangent contacts, texture-aware geometry processing, and stochastic rendering for higher-order diffusion curves. In plain terms, the work is moving toward cases where simple drawings meet demanding pipelines: animation editing, CAD-like surface intersection, 3D-to-2D conversion, textured shape processing, and smooth vector color rendering. The change is reliability under ambiguity: preserving layers, crossings, appearance, and boundary behavior when the input is incomplete, crowded, or numerically delicate.

limits and assumptions

These family claims depend on the input having enough structure for the chosen checks to mean something. Stroke correspondence still assumes that there is a recoverable relation between drawings, even when some marks are hidden. Planar maps and intersection methods assume curves and surfaces are described accurately enough that crossings, loops, and tangencies can be detected rather than buried in bad input. Texture-aware processing assumes appearance can be carried through vertex colors without losing the details that matter for the later tool. Diffusion-curve rendering assumes the boundary conditions describe the intended smooth color behavior. The evidence shows approaches and claimed contributions, but it does not prove broad performance, artist workflow quality, or failure behavior on every messy drawing, noisy scan, or extreme geometric case.

problem Making paint-mixing effects look sharp and realistic requires constant heavy computation as you paint.
approach Pre-store how a brush shape moves paint as functions that combine easily without recalculating.
read the full first-principles story
the big picture

The ordinary problem behind Mixwell is paint-like material on a 2D canvas being pushed by a cylindrical brush tine. In a production scene, this is not a decorative data problem; it affects whether a shape, motion, image, or material can be edited, streamed, rendered, simulated, or physically trusted.
